chapter_theme: On the eve of entering Madurai, the Brahmin Maadalan recounts Kovalan's good deeds (naming his daughter Manimekalai after the goddess who saved an ancestor for his gifts, saving a Brahmin from an elephant, paying for a Brahmin wife's expiation, offering his life to the spirit for a false witness) and asks whether his suffering is the fruit of a former birth; Kovalan tells a dream of ruin and release, and Kavunthi entrusts Kannaki to the herdswoman Maadari, praising her as a deity and binding Maadari to the charge with a Jain tale of a monkey raised to the gods by a housewife's gift.

cast.role: merchant of Puhar, Kannaki's husband, now at the ascetics' grove outside Madurai
Kovalan's wife, entrusted by Kavunthi to the herdswoman Maadari
the Jain woman ascetic (மாதவத் தாட்டி, காவுந்தி ஐயை) who has led the couple to Madurai
Brahmin of Thalaichengaanam, returning from pilgrimage to Kumari, who knows Kovalan's past deeds
the old herdswoman of Madurai to whom Kannaki is entrusted
the dancer of Puhar, mother of Kovalan's daughter Manimekalai
the elder courtesans who propose to name Madhavi's daughter
the sea goddess, Kovalan's family deity, who at Indra's command saved a shipwrecked ancestor
the aged Brahmin, coming to receive gifts, whom Kovalan saved from an elephant
the rogue elephant that seized the Brahmin
the Brahmin who left his wife and went north after the mongoose's death
the Brahmin's wife who sought someone to take the fruit of her wrong deed
the poor man who bore false witness against a chaste wife
the spirit of Puhar's crossroads that seizes false witnesses with its noose and devours them
the mother (or elder sister) of the false witness seized by the spirit
the herdsmen of Madurai carrying axes and pot-slings who walk with Maadari
the herdswomen who walk with Maadari
the Jain charanas (wandering sages) who preach dharma under the asoka at Puhar; their chief (இறையோன்) tells the monkey's story
the Jain lay hearers at Puhar
the god, once Saayalan's monkey, who appears with a monkey's hand on one side
the wife of the merchant Etti Saayalan of Puhar, who raised the monkey and gave gifts in its name
the town monkey that ate the sage's leftovers
the great ascetic fed at Saayalan's house, who bids the wife cherish the monkey

silappathikaram:15:1-20.reading: Having seen Madurai, whose kings' straight sceptre, cool umbrella and victorious spear keep a city that has never had to flee, Kovalan returns to the grove of the ascetics' outer quarter and tells Kavunthi of the evil-free city and the Pandya's might; meanwhile the Brahmin Maadalan of Thalaichengaanam, returning from circling the sage's hill and bathing at Kumari, enters the grove to rest, Kovalan bows at his feet, and the Brahmin begins to speak.
silappathikaram:15:1-20.nuance: Kovalan's report of a Madurai 'free of evil' (தீதுதீர் மதுரை) and of the straightness of its kings' sceptre (கோலின் செம்மை) is the last praise of the Pandya before the killing; the next kaathai will show that sceptre bend on him. Line 7 calls the outer quarter the place of those with dharma-bearing hearts, which line 107 turns into the reason Kovalan must leave it.
silappathikaram:15:1-20.unit_note: Boundary moved: the old first unit ended at line 16 in mid-sentence (தாழ்பொழி லாங்கண், 'in that grove'); the unit now runs to line 20, where the narration closes with உரைப்போன் and Maadalan's speech begins.
silappathikaram:15:1-20.event: Kovalan returns from seeing Madurai to the ascetics' grove and tells Kavunthi of it; the Brahmin Maadalan arrives from Kumari and Kovalan bows to him.

silappathikaram:15:21-41.reading: Maadalan recalls the day the elder courtesans proposed to name the infant daughter of Madhavi, and Kovalan said that an ancestor of his, shipwrecked at midnight on the sea, had been kept afloat because of his meritorious gifts until the goddess Manimekalai came at Indra's bidding, told him not to fear because the merit of his great giving does not fail, and saved him; so the child must bear the name of that family deity, and a thousand courtesans hailed her Manimekalai while Kovalan, with Madhavi, poured gold from his hands.
silappathikaram:15:21-41.nuance: This is the first naming of Manimekalai in the epic, and it ties her name to a sea goddess who rescues for merit, the role the goddess plays for Manimekalai herself in the sequel. The rescue is credited to giving (புண்ணிய தானம், பெருந் தானம்), not to devotion, and the goddess acts on Indra's command (இந்திரன் ஏவலின்).
silappathikaram:15:21-41.unit_note: Boundary moved: the unit begins at line 21 with Maadalan's speech (the old unit began at 17, mid-narration) and ends at line 41, where the naming scene closes with the gold poured out (பொழிய); the next clause opens a new episode, the Brahmin who came for gifts.
silappathikaram:15:21-41.event: At the naming of Madhavi's daughter Kovalan has her called Manimekalai after the goddess who saved his shipwrecked ancestor, and pours out gold gifts.

claims.claim: the merit of great giving does not fail and brings rescue in disaster

silappathikaram:15:42-53.reading: Maadalan goes on: on that day an aged Brahmin, bent and leaning on a staff, coming to receive gifts, was seized by a rogue elephant that had thrown off its driver, and Kovalan, shouting, freed the man from its trunk, entered between its tusks, sat on its neck like a vidyadhara on a black hill and tamed it, and Maadalan hails him as the compassionate warrior who subdued the elephant.
silappathikaram:15:42-53.nuance: The vocative கருணை மறவ joins compassion and martial courage in a merchant; the feat is told as one more of Kovalan's good deeds in a list that will end in the question why such a man suffers (lines 91 to 94).
silappathikaram:15:42-53.unit_note: Boundary moved: the old units 33-48 and 49-64 split the elephant episode in mid-sentence at line 48; this unit runs from line 42 (the Brahmin's arrival) to line 53, which closes the episode with the vocative கருணை மறவ.
silappathikaram:15:42-53.event: A rogue elephant seizes an old Brahmin who came for gifts, and Kovalan frees him and tames the elephant.

silappathikaram:15:54-75.reading: Maadalan tells how a Brahmin, after the mongoose they kept as a child came to its death, left for the north with his grieving wife following, telling her that living on food from her hand was no longer his duty and giving her a leaf written in Sanskrit to be placed in the hands of men who know duty; she went from house to house through the merchants' streets crying for someone to take the fruit of her deed, and Kovalan called her, heard her trouble, took the leaf, gave her wealth, had her wrong removed by gifts as the Brahmins' books lay down, brought back her husband and set them on a good path, and Maadalan hails him as one whose wealth never fails.
silappathikaram:15:54-75.nuance: The text says only that the mongoose came to its death (பெரும்பிறிது ஆக) and that the wife was scorned (எள்ளிய); that she herself caused the death is implied by line 71, which calls her the one who did a harmful deed (தீத்திறம் புரிந்தோள்), not told. Kovalan does not take the sin on himself: he pays for the expiation the Brahmins' law books prescribe, and the merchant's wealth is what makes the rite possible.
silappathikaram:15:54-75.unit_note: Boundary moved: the unit runs from line 54 (the mongoose) to line 75, where the episode closes with the vocative செல்லாச் செல்வ; the old boundary at 64/65 fell between her cry and her answer.
silappathikaram:15:54-75.event: A Brahmin leaves his wife after their pet mongoose dies; Kovalan pays for her expiation by gifts and brings her husband back.

claims.claim: a husband may refuse to live on the food of a wife who has done a grave wrong
a wrong deed's sin is removed by gifts made as the Brahmins' law books prescribe

silappathikaram:15:76-94.reading: Maadalan tells how a poor man who bore false witness to a chaste wife's husband about what he did not know was caught in the noose of the spirit that beats and devours, how Kovalan, seeing the man's mother grieve, ran to the spirit and offered his own life for the man's, and how the spirit refused, saying it had no way of taking a good life for a hell-bound one and losing the higher state, and struck the man dead before him; Kovalan went away with the grieving woman and for many years fed the dead man's kin, and Maadalan, having listed these good deeds of this birth, asks whether it is the fruit of a former birth that Kovalan now suffers alone with his jewel of a wife.
silappathikaram:15:76-94.nuance: Maadalan's question (உம்மைப் பயன்கொல்) is the first time in the Madurai book that a character reasons from undeserved suffering to a deed of a former birth: the good deeds of this life (இம்மைச் செய்தன யானறி நல்வினை) are known and cannot explain it, so the cause must lie further back. It is put as a question, not a verdict. The spirit's refusal shows its justice cannot be bought even with a good man's life. விருத்தகோபால (line 94) is an address to Kovalan; whether விருத்த means 'old', 'vowed' or something else here is not clear. Whether தவ்வை (line 80) is the man's mother or his elder sister is not settled by the line.
silappathikaram:15:76-94.unit_note: Boundary moved: the old boundary at 82/83 cut Kovalan's offer from the spirit's answer; the unit runs from line 76 (the chaste wife) to line 94, where Maadalan's question ends with வினவ.
silappathikaram:15:76-94.event: The spirit seizes a false witness; Kovalan offers his life for the man's, the spirit refuses and kills him, and Kovalan supports the dead man's family for years.

claims.claim: one who bears false witness is seized and devoured by the spirit
a good life may not be taken in exchange for a sinner's, for that would cost the higher state
suffering not explained by the good deeds of this life is the fruit of deeds of a former birth

silappathikaram:15:95-106.reading: Kovalan answers with a dream he had at midnight as vivid as waking: in the guarded city of the king, because of a petty man, his wife fell into trembling distress, his garment was seized and he rode a horned beast; then, with his wife, he reached the state of those who have cut their bonds, Kama flung his flower arrows on the bare ground and stood helpless, and Madhavi gave Manimekalai before the virtuous one of the shining Bodhi tree; and he fears that something bad will soon come.
silappathikaram:15:95-106.nuance: The dream compresses the rest of the story in order: the petty man (குறுமகன்) is the goldsmith to come, the seized garment and the ride on a horned beast are signs of death, the couple's reaching the state of the unbound (பிணிப்பறுத்தோர் தம் பெற்றி) is their afterlife, and Madhavi's giving her daughter before the Buddha (போதி அறவோன்) is the Manimekalai's opening. Kovalan reads only the first part, as a coming harm; he does not answer Maadalan's question about a former birth.
silappathikaram:15:95-106.unit_note: Unit split: the old unit 83-98 and 99-113 cut the dream at line 98; this unit runs from line 95 (கோவலன் கூறும்) to line 106, where the dream closes with கடிதீங் குறுமென.
silappathikaram:15:95-106.event: Kovalan tells Maadalan a dream of his wife's distress, his own seizure and death-ride, and Madhavi's giving their daughter to the Buddha.

silappathikaram:15:107-114.reading: Kavunthi and Maadalan tell Kovalan that this outer quarter is fit only for those on the path of dharma, that the merchants of the inner city will receive him at the mention of his name, and that he should enter great Madurai with his wife before the sun sets.
silappathikaram:15:107-114.nuance: Lines 107 and 108 make the ascetics' quarter unfit for a householder, so the couple must leave the place the narration called 'dharma-bearing' (line 7) for the city where the killing will happen. அரைசர் பின்னோர் ('those after the kings') names the merchant class by rank.
silappathikaram:15:107-114.unit_note: Unit split: the unit runs from line 107 to line 114, where the sentence closes with கூறுங் காலை; the old unit 99-113 ended one line before the verb.
silappathikaram:15:107-114.event: Kavunthi and Maadalan urge Kovalan to leave the ascetics' quarter and enter Madurai with his wife before sunset.

silappathikaram:15:115-130.reading: As they speak, the old herdswoman Maadari, coming back from offering milk rice to the yakshi of the outer quarter, worships Kavunthi; Kavunthi, judging that the life of herders who tend cows and give their yield has no crookedness and that this old woman is blameless and kind, tells her that when Kovalan's people hear whose son he is they will receive him like a guest of great worth, and that until he enters a rich man's house she gives Kannaki to Maadari as a charge in her keeping.
silappathikaram:15:115-130.nuance: This is the act that names the kaathai: அடைக்கலம் here is a ward placed in another's protection, the sense the rest of the chapter builds on, not the Saiva self-surrender to the Lord that the concept usually tags elsewhere. Kavunthi's trust rests on a judgment of the herders' way of life as a whole (கோவலர் வாழ்க்கை), not on knowledge of Maadari herself. பூங்கண் இயக்கி is a yakshi goddess, and Maadari, a herdswoman, worships her and a Jain ascetic alike.
silappathikaram:15:115-130.unit_note: Boundary moved: the unit begins at line 115 (அறம்புரி நெஞ்சின்), with Maadari's arrival, since line 114 closes the sentence of Kavunthi's and Maadalan's advice; it ends at line 130, where Kavunthi's entrusting closes with அடைக்கலந் தந்தேன்.
silappathikaram:15:115-130.event: Maadari worships Kavunthi, who judges her trustworthy and entrusts Kannaki to her keeping.

claims.claim: the life of herders who tend cows and give their yield has no crookedness

silappathikaram:15:131-148.reading: Kavunthi tells Maadari to bathe Kannaki, line her eyes, put flowers in her hair, dress her in clean cloth and be her companions, guard and mother; she says the earth never knew this girl's small feet, that in the scorching sun she grieved for her husband's pain and never for her own, that she has seen no goddess fairer than this one who bears the vow of the chastity a wife cannot be without, and asks whether Maadari does not know the good saying that where chaste wives live the sky does not fail, plenty does not falter and the victory of kings does not decay.
silappathikaram:15:131-148.nuance: Kavunthi calls Kannaki a deity (இத்தெய்வம்), the strongest claim yet about her, and grounds it in her bearing pain for her husband and not for herself. The saying of lines 145 to 147 is quoted as common wisdom (அத்தகு நல்லுரை), not as Jain teaching, and it pledges the king's victory to the presence of pathini women: the Pandya of this very city will fall because of one.
silappathikaram:15:131-148.unit_note: Boundary moved: the unit runs from line 131 (the bathing) to line 148, where the saying closes with அறியா யோநீ; the old boundary at 147/148 cut the saying from its question.

claims.claim: chastity is the one thing a wife cannot be without
where chaste wives live, the rain does not fail, plenty does not falter and the king's victory does not decay

silappathikaram:15:149-162.reading: Kavunthi adds that a charge held for the ascetics, however small, yields very great joy, and tells a story: at Puhar, under the flowering asoka on the shining stone seat the world's ascetics had set up, where the charanas preached dharma, there appeared a god with a body bright as a rainbow, garlands and gold ornaments, a form the world cannot see, with a black-fingered monkey's hand on one part of him, and when the lay hearers worshipped the charanas and asked why he came, the chief of them spoke.
silappathikaram:15:149-162.nuance: தவத்தோர் அடைக்கலம் can be read as a charge entrusted by ascetics, as Kavunthi has just entrusted Kannaki, or as refuge given to ascetics; the story that follows (a monkey that a sage bids a housewife cherish) fits the first. The setting is Jain throughout: the asoka (பிண்டி), the charanas (சாரணர்), the lay hearers (சாவகர்).
silappathikaram:15:149-162.unit_note: Boundary moved: the unit begins at line 149 with Kavunthi's maxim (the old unit began at 148, the last line of the saying); its end at 162 is unchanged.
silappathikaram:15:149-162.event: At Puhar a god with a monkey's hand appears before the Jain charanas, and the lay hearers ask why.

claims.claim: keeping a charge entrusted by ascetics, however small, brings very great joy

silappathikaram:15:163-173.reading: The chief charana tells that in the house of Etti Saayalan, where many fasting ascetics came, as the lady of the house was receiving a great ascetic, a small town monkey crept in, touched his feet, drank a little of the leftover food and the water he had spilled, and looked up into his face, and the sage, pleased, told the lady to cherish it as her own children.
silappathikaram:15:163-173.nuance: The monkey's merit begins with eating an ascetic's leftovers (மிச்சில்) and looking into his face, and with the sage's word that turns an animal into a ward: the story is built to fit Kavunthi's maxim of a charge held for ascetics.
silappathikaram:15:163-173.event: A monkey eats a visiting ascetic's leftovers in Saayalan's house, and the ascetic bids the housewife raise it as her child.

silappathikaram:15:174-191.reading: The charana goes on: keeping the sage's true word, the woman cared for the monkey, and when it died she set aside a share of her gifts in its name so its evil might end; so it was born the son of Uttara Kauttan in Varanasi of the middle country, excellent in form, fortune and understanding, made many gifts, and after thirty-two years died and took the form of a god; and, saying that all the fruit of this was the virtue of the gift of the woman who had raised him, and that the monkey's small hand on part of the god's body shows he became this form through Saayalan's wife's gift, the chief showed him to the hearers, and the god's son appeared.
silappathikaram:15:174-191.nuance: Merit here passes from one being to another: the woman's gift, made for the monkey's share (அதற்கொரு கூறு), raises it to a human birth, and that birth's own gifts raise it to the gods. The god's body keeps the monkey's hand, so the reward of merit is itself a birth that still bears the mark of the one before. That the woman made the gift so that the monkey's evil should end (தீதறுக) treats an animal birth as the fruit of evil to be cleared.
silappathikaram:15:174-191.event: The charana tells how the monkey, through the housewife's gift in its name, was reborn a prince and then a god, and shows the god to the hearers.

claims.claim: a gift made in another being's name can raise that being to a better birth
the gifts of a human birth lead after death to a god's form

silappathikaram:15:192-199.reading: Kavunthi ends that those who took the charanas' good words as precious and turned to dharma, the ascetics of that city, the lay hearers who lived restrained lives and the merchant and his wife of the gift, reached the final world of unbroken joy; and she tells Maadari that, having heard this, she should go with the girl without delay.
silappathikaram:15:192-199.nuance: The giving couple reach not another heaven but the final world (முடிவுலகு), and the line ties this to hearing the charanas and turning to dharma (அறந்தலைப் பட்டோர்), not to the gift alone. Kavunthi tells the story to bind Maadari to her charge; the story promises great joy to the keeper, which the later kaathais do not give Maadari.
silappathikaram:15:192-199.unit_note: Boundary moved: the unit runs from line 192 to line 199, where Kavunthi's speech closes with நீபோ கென்றே; the old unit 192-207 ran on into the narration of Maadari's walk home.

claims.claim: those who heed the charanas' teaching and turn to dharma, lay givers among them, reach the final world of unending joy

silappathikaram:15:200-219.reading: When Kavunthi has spoken, Maadari praises her gladly and, as the sun goes down and cows call for their calves, sets out with the wise young Kannaki, herdsmen with axes on their shoulders and pot-slings and herdswomen around them, passes through the gate of Madurai, bristling beyond its moat with the fort's engines, bows, slings, boiling oil and molten metal, hooks, stakes and iron bars, spears and every other device, where the day's banners wave, and enters her house, holding to what she had taken on.
silappathikaram:15:200-219.nuance: The long list of war engines on Madurai's wall (lines 207 to 216) is the city's defence against siege at the very moment it admits the woman whose wrong will burn it. Among the engines is a black-fingered monkey (கருவிர லூகம்), set against the black-fingered monkey (கருவிரற் குரங்கு, line 159) of Kavunthi's tale. The closing word கொள்கையிற் புணர்ந்து says Maadari took on the charge as her resolve.
silappathikaram:15:200-219.unit_note: Boundary moved: the unit begins at line 200 (கவுந்தி கூற), where the narration resumes, and runs to the end; the old boundary at 207/208 fell in the middle of the list of engines.
silappathikaram:15:200-219.event: Maadari takes Kannaki through Madurai's fortified gate at sunset and brings her home.

links.note: Kovalan reports a Madurai free of evil whose kings' sceptre is straight (கோலின் செம்மை, தீதுதீர் மதுரை); the Pandya, after killing him, declares himself the thief and his guarding failed.
links.teaches: The straightness of the Pandya sceptre is first vouched for by the man it will kill, on the day before his death, so the epic lets the victim's trust in the city's justice set the measure by which the king condemns himself.

links.note: Maadalan, finding no cause for Kovalan's suffering in his good deeds of this life, asks whether it is the fruit of a former birth; the patikam's goddess names that cause, a curse from a former birth.
links.teaches: The epic reaches its doctrine of former deeds by elimination: a witness who knows only Kovalan's good acts can explain his ruin only by a past birth, and the patikam later confirms the guess with a named curse, so the karmic cause is offered as what remains when the visible life acquits the sufferer.

links.note: The crossroads spirit of Puhar announces that it seizes false witnesses and others with its noose and devours them; here it seizes one and refuses Kovalan's offer of his own life in exchange.
links.teaches: The spirit's announced punishment proves rigid in practice: it will not take a good man's life even when he offers it, so the pair shows its justice as exact matching of deed to doer, with no place for the substitution that Kovalan's generosity proposes.

links.note: Kovalan dreams of his wife's distress, his seized garment and a death-ride, then release and his daughter's renunciation; the Pandya queen dreams of the umbrella and sceptre falling and the sky in disorder.
links.teaches: The same ruin is dreamed from both sides of the verdict: the victim's dream runs past death into release and his daughter's turn to the Buddha, the queen's stops at the fall of the sceptre, so the dreams divide between them the epic's two morals of ripening deeds and failed kingship.

links.note: The couplet says a wife who worships her husband rather than a god can bid the rain fall; Kavunthi calls Kannaki a deity fairer than any she has seen and quotes a saying that where chaste wives live the sky never fails and kings' victory never decays.
links.teaches: Where the couplet keeps the wife below the gods yet gives her command of the rain, Kavunthi makes the chaste wife herself the deity and extends her power from rain to the king's victory, which is the very extension the epic will turn against the Pandya when that power destroys his city.

gains.a: Kavunthi's saying gains a source for its rain clause in a couplet that ties the wife's power to her refusal of other gods
gains.b: the couplet gains a reading in which the chaste wife's power reaches past nature to the fortunes of kings, and so becomes a threat as well as a blessing

links.note: Kavunthi quotes the saying that where chaste wives live the kings' victory does not decay; the patikam says that because Kannaki was a pathini she burned Madurai and the Pandya fell.
links.teaches: The saying Kavunthi offers as a pledge of the king's safety is reversed in the same city, where a pathini's presence ends the king, so the pair shows that the epic makes the chaste wife's power conditional on the king's justice rather than a blessing that protects any throne.

links.note: The couplet holds that giving is good even if there were no higher world; the charana proves the worth of a gift by showing the god it produced, with the monkey's hand still on him.
links.teaches: The Kural deliberately cuts giving loose from any reward in a higher world, while the Jain tale makes a visible heavenly body the evidence for the gift's worth, so the pair separates two defences of giving, one that needs no world beyond and one that rests on it.

gains.a: the tale's proof by reward is set against a view that does not need the proof, which shows how much its case rests on the heaven it displays
gains.b: the couplet's hypothetical 'even if there were no higher world' gains a concrete rival: a contemporary teaching that answers the hypothetical by producing the higher world as witness

links.note: Tirumular says merit and sin both come with one into birth and both must be cut at the root to reach the Lord; the Jain tale shows merit carrying a monkey to a human birth and then to a god's body that keeps the monkey's hand.
links.teaches: The god who still bears a monkey's hand makes visible Tirumular's point that merit, too, works by giving births: the reward of the gift is another body marked by the last one, which is why the Saiva verse ranks merit as a bond to be uprooted rather than a road to the Lord.

gains.a: the tale's god with the monkey's hand gains a reading as a sign that merit's fruit is still a birth, not only a proof of the gift's power
gains.b: Tirumular's abstract claim that merit binds gains a concrete image of a merit-made body that carries the history of its former birth

links.note: The Jain debater in the Manimekalai says release is to block the inflow of both good and bad deeds and wear out past ones; the Jain charana of the Silappathikaram tells a gift whose merit leads to a god's birth.
links.teaches: Held together, the Jain doctrine stated in debate and the Jain tale told for lay hearers show the two levels of the same teaching: the doctrine counts good deeds among the bonds, while the tale for householders displays the heavenly birth that good deeds bring, and Kavunthi reserves release itself for those who turn to dharma (line 197).

links.note: The couplet calls a fort that which cannot be taken by siege, storm or work on those inside; Madurai's gate is lined with every engine against attack as Kannaki passes through it.
links.teaches: The epic fills Madurai's walls with the defences the Kural's fort requires at the very moment it lets in the woman whose wrong will burn the city from within, so the pair shows a danger the couplet's three threats do not name: an injustice of the king's own that no engine on the wall can repel.

gains.a: the list of engines gains a measure: by the Kural's standard the city is a perfect fort, which sharpens the irony of its fall
gains.b: the couplet's account of impregnability gains a case where the fort is lost through no siege at all, but through the king's own wrong

new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own word (பத்தினிப் பெண்டிர், line 147; பத்தினி, line 76); id as declared in silappathikaram ch001

source_issues: Lineation: the edition's printed last line is 215 against 219 lines as shown, so its printed numbers run four behind by the end; line numbers here are the kaathai's own as `show` prints them.
Chapter 20 of this marking is the fifteenth kaathai (அடைக்கலக் காதை, unit ids silappathikaram:15:...); the brief's 'Silappathikaram 20' (the plea before the Pandya) is kaathai 20, chapter 26.
Line 94 விருத்தகோபால: the word division and sense of விருத்த are unclear.
Line 80 பட்டோன் றவ்வை: தவ்வை may be the man's mother or elder sister.
